About: Tachyon Causality Violation

Source

Lecture
18 — Causality & Tachyons
Simulation
Simulation 0 — Tachyon causality violation on a Minkowski diagram (guided-inquiry)
Concept
A signal from A ("A sends") to B ("B receives") outside A's light cone must be superluminal (v > c). For such a spacelike pair a boost reverses the time-order (Δct′ flips sign), and a superluminal return signal then arrives before A sent — effect precedes cause.
Serves
Causal structure of the light cone (timelike vs spacelike); superluminal signalling ⇒ frame-dependent time order; the acausal round-trip loop; why tachyons would need m² < 0; the deep link to the relativity of simultaneity (tilted S′ axes).
Inquiry
When does the A→B signal need v > c? At which boost does Δct′ change sign? Can the return signal reach A before it sent — and what would that mean?
Misconception
"A fast-enough signal is fine — going faster than light just means arriving sooner; it can't break cause and effect."

Tachyon Causality Violation

Event A on the x axis, its future light cone opening at 45°, and a signal running out to event B beyond the cone's edge.

Welcome toTachyon causality violation

Two events joined by a faster-than-light signal — does every frame agree which came first?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two events, two frames

Let’s meet the two events. Event A at (x, ct) = (0.00, 0.00) sends a signal received at event B at (3.21, 4.70). Their separation is Δs² = −Δct² + Δx², negative when B lies inside A's light cone and positive when it lies outside. A second observer S′ moves at v/c relative to S and, for the same two events, measures Δct′ = γ(Δct − (v/c)·Δx).

2 · Order inside the cone

Let’s start with a signal slower than light. B lies inside A’s light cone: Δs² = −11.79, and the A→B signal travels at 0.68 c. Taking every frame with |v/c| < 1, what do you think becomes of the order of A and B?

3 · Outside the cone

Now let’s push B out past the edge. B now sits outside A’s light cone at (5.00, 2.00): Δs² = +21.00, and the A→B signal travels at 2.50 c. Look at Δct′ = γ(Δct − (v/c)·Δx): what do you think that has changed?

4 · Moving B further out

Let’s see how far that goes. For this pair Δct′ passes through zero at v/c = 0.40. Drag B further from A along x, holding Δct at +2.00. What do you expect to happen to the boost at which the order reverses?

5 · The reply

Now for the twist: a reply. At v/c = 0.60 the order has reversed: in S′, B receives before A sends. B now answers at v₂ = 3.00 c in S′, meeting A’s worldline at E₃ with ct₃ = 0.33 — still above A. What do you think would bring ct₃ below A?

6 · The antitelephone

Let’s step back and see what you’ve found. A signal crossing a spacelike interval has no frame-independent direction in time — that is the content of Δs² > 0, and the tilted S′ lines of constant time are where it shows. Add a reply and the round trip lands on the sender's own worldline before the sending event: the tachyonic antitelephone. The light cone bounds causal order, not merely speed.

And one last thing to think about: a particle permanently above c — a tachyon — would need m² < 0 in E² = p²c² + m²c⁴.

The Physics

Causality and tachyons · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim draws two events, A and B, on a spacetime diagram and lets a second observer, S′, move past at any speed below c. It tests whether the time order of A and B depends on the observer, and what a faster-than-light reply would do to cause and effect.

What you'll learn

  • What the interval Δs² says about two events, and how it sorts signals by speed.
  • How the time order of two events depends on the observer's frame, and for which pairs.
  • How the boost needed to reverse that order depends on how far apart the events are.
  • How a faster-than-light reply and a reversed order combine, and what mass a tachyon would need.
Frame S: event A sends a signal to event B. The teal axes belong to S′, a frame moving along x relative to S.

What's on screen

  • A (blue dot) sends the signal, from (x, ct) = (0.00, 0.00).
  • B (rose dot) receives the signal, at (3.21, 4.70). Both dots drag.
  • Light cone (dashed yellow): 45° lines through A.
  • A → B arrow and tag: the signal speed |Δx/Δct|, green, yellow or red by interval class.
  • S′ grid and axes (teal): tilt as v/c changes. The grey grid is S.
  • Tags top-left: v/c and the time order each frame sees. The Readings panel holds the numbers.
  • Return signal on: a dashed pink arrow from B to the amber triangle E₃, and a ⚠ LOOP tag when E₃ falls before A.
See itLoad the sim's opening pair at v/c = 0. Watch for: the yellow light cone through A, with B (rose) inside it and the arrow from A to B.

03

The interval and the light cone

Frame S describes the pair by Δct = ctB − ctA and Δx = xB − xA. With time measured as ct, light runs at 45°. The interval of the pair is:

Timelike pairs are negative, spacelike pairs positive, null pairs zero.
  • The same in every frame. Frame S′ computes Δct′² − Δx′² for the same two events and gets the same number. The Readings panel shows both.
  • It sorts the signal by speed. A signal that carries A's influence to B has average speed |Δx/Δct| in S. Δs² < 0 means that is below c, so B lies inside A's light cone. Δs² > 0 means it is above c, so B lies outside.
  • On the cone, Δs² = 0 and the signal moves at c.
See itLoad the pair with B inside the cone. Watch for: a green signal tag at 0.68 c, and Δs² = −11.79 in the card.
See itLoad the pair with B outside the cone. Watch for: the signal tag turning red at 2.50 c, and Δs² = +21.00 in the card.
04

Which events a boost can reorder

Frame S′ moves along x at v = βc relative to S, with γ = 1/√(1 − β²). For the same two events, S′ measures the time separation:

Δct′ > 0 means A comes before B in S′.
  • γ is positive, so the sign of Δct′ is the sign of Δct − βΔx.
  • Inside the cone, |Δx| < |Δct|. Since |β| < 1, |βΔx| stays below |Δct|, so Δct′ keeps the sign of Δct. Every frame agrees which event comes first.
  • Outside the cone, |Δx| > |Δct|. Now βΔx can exceed Δct while |β| is still below 1, so Δct′ can change sign. S′ then sees B before A.

The tags on the canvas and the Readings panel print the order each frame sees.

See itBoost the inside pair to v/c = 0.80. Watch for: S′ still reading A before B, with Δct′ = +3.55.
See itBoost the outside pair to v/c = 0.60. Watch for: S′ reading B before A, the ⚠ order flipped tag, and Δct′ = −1.25.
05

How much boost it takes

Setting Δct′ = 0 gives the boost at which A and B become simultaneous in S′: βflip = Δct/Δx. A boost of the same sign and larger size reverses the order.

The line of constant ct′ through B, for B = (5.00, 2.00). At β = 0.40 it passes through A.
  • Farther apart, easier. βflip falls as Δx grows at fixed Δct. For Δct = 2.00 it is 0.40 at Δx = 5.00 and 0.29 at Δx = 7.00.
  • Direction matters. β must have the sign of βflip. A boost the other way only makes Δct′ larger.
  • Inside the cone there is none. There |Δct/Δx| exceeds 1, which no boost reaches.

06

How a faster reply closes a loop

Turn on Return signal. B answers with a reply that moves at v₂ in S′, aimed at A's worldline x = xA. It arrives at event E₃, which the sim transforms back to S:

d = ±1 is the direction of the reply in S′. The threshold form assumes A at x = 0, B to the right of A, and Δx > Δct > 0.
  • A and E₃ share a worldline. A is at rest in S, so E₃ sits straight above or below A, and every frame agrees which comes first. If ct₃ < ctA, the reply arrives before A sent the message: a loop.
  • The loop needs more boost than the flip. For B to the right of A, βloop is above βflip, and a faster reply lowers it toward βflip.
  • Example, B = (5.00, 2.00), v₂ = 3.00 c: βloop = 11/17 ≈ 0.65. At β = 0.60, ct₃ = +0.33. At β = 0.80, ct₃ = −1.18.
  • For a pair inside the cone, ct₃ stays after A at every v/c and v₂ the sim allows.

The argument assumes that if a faster-than-light signal is allowed, it is allowed in every frame.

See itBoost to v/c = 0.60 with the reply on. Watch for: E₃ still above A, and the Readings line reading no loop.
See itRaise the boost to v/c = 0.80. Watch for: E₃ below A, and the red ⚠ LOOP tag on the canvas.
07

What a tachyon would need

For a particle with mass, p = γmv and E = γmc² give v = pc²/E. Combined with E² = p²c² + m²c⁴, a speed above c forces:

Straight from the course derivation. A hypothetical particle with m² < 0 is called a tachyon.
  • A tachyon needs a negative m². v > c means pc > E, so m²c⁴ = E² − p²c² is negative and m is not a real number.
  • Speeding up an ordinary particle does not get there. E = γmc² grows without limit as v → c, so no finite energy reaches c, let alone passes it.

The sim draws signals, not particles, so it shows what any faster-than-light signal would do to cause and effect, not a tachyon itself.

08

Where it matters

  • Accelerators. A 6.5 TeV proton in the LHC has γ ≈ 6900 and moves within about one part in 10⁸ of c. Added energy raises γ, not the speed.
  • The OPERA neutrinos. In 2011 that experiment reported neutrinos arriving about 60 ns earlier than light would. The cause was traced to timing equipment, a loose fibre-optic connection and a clock fault, and the result was withdrawn. The loop argument is part of why the claim needed such a check.
  • Cherenkov light. In water, light travels at about 0.75 c. A particle faster than that makes a blue glow. It is still slower than c, so no light cone is crossed.
Go deeper: tachyons in field theory
  • In quantum field theory, a field with m² < 0 describes an unstable point, not particles faster than light. The field rolls down to a stable minimum, and the excitations there have positive m².
  • The Higgs field is the standard example: its potential has this shape near zero field, before the electroweak symmetry breaks.
09

Summary

In one line. Inside the light cone every observer agrees which event comes first; outside it a boost can reverse the order, and a faster-than-light reply can then arrive before the message that caused it.

Key points

  • Δs² is the same in every frame, and its sign says whether B is inside, on or outside A's light cone.
  • Δct′ = γ(Δct − βΔx) can change sign for |β| < 1 only when |Δx| > |Δct|, at βflip = Δct/Δx.
  • A reply at v₂ in S′ arrives before the message once β passes βloop, which is above βflip.
  • A particle faster than c would need m² < 0.

Common mix-ups

  • "A moving observer can reorder any two events." Only pairs outside each other's light cones. Inside, every observer agrees.
  • "Anything faster than c breaks causality." Only a signal that carries influence does. A laser spot sweeping across a distant screen can move faster than c, because each position of the spot does not cause the next.
  • "This sim shows tachyons cannot exist." It shows what a usable faster-than-light signal would do to cause and effect. It tests no particle.

Things to try on your own

  • Drag B to (7.00, 2.00) and find where Δct′ changes sign on the v/c slider. Compare it with Δct/Δx.
  • Load the outside pair, set v/c = 0.60, turn on Return signal, and raise v₂ until ct₃ drops below zero.
  • Drag B well inside the cone, sweep v/c across its whole range, and watch Δct′.
